utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, may we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Thomas Laugel, Jaclyn Fortini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, and Jolana Makraiova as our intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just one brief technical matter before we bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I have been reminded that the Prosecution needs to re-tender exhibit 65 ter 00079.1. This is the part of the book that has now been reduced to the part that was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document shall be assigned Exhibit Number P2890. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Excellency. May I remind you that you're still on your oath. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings. I'll ask you a few questions today. If any of my questions aren't clear, please feel free to ask for a clarification and I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday some questions about Croats and Serbs as ethnic groups. Did Slovenes also comprise an ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Yugoslav terminology they were a nation as were the Serbs and as were the Croats. But the Slovenes are in so far different as their language is clearly a different language from what used to be called Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness, please, be asked to come closer to the microphones. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So in that sense, they would be even more distinct from the other groups that comprised or lived in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And why did they want to secede from the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this is a question concerning history of our times, and this is a long story in Yugoslavia. But you might be aware that Milosevic had organised changes of government first in the two autonomous provinces of Serbia, in Vojvodina and in Kosovo, and that he had sent his people, there was an expression [B/C/S spoken], the people have happened, into Montenegro and replaced the leadership there by people of his own. When he sent the people to Slovenia the Slovenes closed the border and then Serbia broke off relations with Slovenia, so this was an ongoing process, and I can only recommend you to read the 500 pages of my book for a good answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say that the process leading to the secession of Slovenia from Yugoslavia was a movement of national self-determination?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That thought was said, but there was always in public international law this difference between self-determination, on the one side, and the unity of states on the other, and this was one of the big problems in dealing with the Yugoslav crisis. But, in the end, I think the developments on the ground went in the direction that a separation became unavoidable. I mean, after Vukovar you could not save Yugoslavia. You couldn't do it even before but after it was certainly ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's leave aside public international law. My question really concerns what is animating or driving the process towards self- -- towards secession and statehood and is it what is driving, and we're taking the case now of Slovenia, is it what's driving the movement towards statehood and secession, some sense of collective identity of the people living in that area?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the Slovenes in a way have a different identity. And I remember at one point I sat with some Serbian friends in Belgrade and one of them said, I don't like Slovenes, and as we had spoken Serb, he did not remember that I was German and someone asked him, Why didn't you like Slovenes? Because they are like the Germans. So this was this alpine nature of Slovenia, but the Slovenes had to save their national identity from Germanisation and from Italianisation and that is why they linked up with Yugoslavia after the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: To put the matter shortly, they wanted a separate state to reflect, in some manner, their sense of national identity. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wanted to preserve the national identity and felt that joining Yugoslavia might be the best way at that point in time, after the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would that be in common parlance a movement of national self-determination?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a way, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would the movement that led to the collapse of Czechoslovakia and the separation of Slovakia and the Czech Republic also be an example of statehood arising from a movement of national self-determination?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, I don't want really to be fixed on these ideas because I have myself have slightly different ideas from this, and I mean, as we are hopefully still moving towards more European unity, I think this insistence on the statehood of each nation was not very wise, particularly when you deal with areas that have a population like a leopard skin because this would then inevitably lead to bloodshed. It's interesting, there is a book by Margaret MacMillan, 1919, discussing this national principle introduced by Wilson in his 14 points and the disastrous consequences it had. I mean, if you look at the states that were formed then, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and even the Soviet Union that was formed, not on this basis but also came to being in those years, you see that this did not work and we are on a different way now. But the others, these are more or less political statements that come from an individual's political convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm not trying to get into a normative discussion about the merits of these movements but, rather, a descriptive discussion to understand what we're dealing with. And would you agree that the collapse of Czechoslovakia is the product of at least two movements of national self-determination, namely, the Slovaks and Czechs?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there is a difference between the Slovaks and the Czechs. And the Slovaks again, after the First World War most of them had been under Hungarian rule, joined this Slavic state and later felt they should not stay together with the Czechs, but this was, after all, an agreed divorce and not this madness which we have seen in Yugoslavia. Sorry for the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But the answer is yes to my question, right, that this was a product of movements of national identity wishing to have a reflection in statehood; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That does not mean that agree with it, but it was an effect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I fully understand that you don't agree with it. And would other examples be the movements in Catalonia, Quebec, Kosovo, would those also be examples of movements of national self-determination?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I should not go into these areas of which I'm not particularly knowledgeable. As far as Kosovo is concerned, the Albanians are, of course, a totally different nation from the Slavic nations that Yugoslavia had, and this is a longer story than just the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Croatia's desire to separate from Yugoslavia a product of national self-determination wishes?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Productive in what respect? Producing what?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did it arise from that wish for autonomy to reflect, in some sense, some ethnic sense, some sense of collective ethnic identity.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly the case in Croatia, but there was a predecessors. You might know that after the First World War, the Croatian voters voted against the Yugoslav Vidovdan constitution, and the Croatian Peasants Party under Radic, who was later shot in the Serb Skupstina, was for independent Croatia. Then you had these [indiscernible] 39 which was practically a separation before the Second World War. Then had you this awful NDH --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm going to come to the NDH in a moment. But before we do get to that, let me just put you to the proposition that I was driving at with my previous questions, which is there is no necessary link or there's no necessity in a national self-determination movement to drive out all of those who are not of the ethnicity of the group that is pushing for national self-determination. There's no necessity that that be the case, is it?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you were discussing the independent state of Croatia and, first of all, can I just ask you, what years did that state exist? Let's leave aside all the details, but just what years did that state exist?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April 1941 to the end of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yesterday at 7678, you described that state as: "A very bad Fascist regime."

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why -- why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they had a Fascist system. The leader Ante Pavelic called himself the Poglavnik which is some sort of Fuehrer, and they committed genocidal acts against Serbs but also against Jews and Roma. They committed horrible crimes against Serbs particularly in Western Herzegovina and this was in very clear memory of the Serbs in 1991 and one should be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say "genocidal acts," is it your view that there was a genocide perpetrated against Serbs by that regime?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the definition of genocide again is a rather difficult one. But Serbs were killed massively just for being Serbs and this included women and children and they were partly only thrown into caves in these -- these Karst mountains which they had in Herzegovina, just left there to die. I mean, there is a lot of stories but I was seven years old at that time. I don't know -- what I know, I know from books and from people who have seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were they closely allied and aligned with the policies of Nazi Germany?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, there was absolutely no need to tell the Croats to persecute Jews. They did it by themselves. This is different from countries where the Nazis imposed their horrible policy on other nations. And in so far, I think the Pavelic state was worse than most of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You're saying that they did it willingly and enthusiastically?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was the chequer-board symbol displayed as a symbol of that state along with the swastika?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the chequer-board symbol is a very old symbol. It has been used in Croatia in the Middle Ages. I have seen myself pictures of that age. It was used by the NDH, that's correct, but it had, of course, a different history than the swastika which Hitler had, I don't know from where, could be from out of nowhere because there was absolutely no tradition for the swastika in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the swastika, of course, is a Buddhist symbol --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- long predates its use by the Nazis so there is a history of appropriation of symbols. But my question to you was whether or not the chequer-board symbol was used alongside the swastika as a symbol representing that state, that regime, of the NDH?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Pavelic used the swastika at all, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at the end of World War II, did Tito suppress the use of the chequer-board symbol?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know positively but that should be natural that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why would you say it would be natural that he would do that?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a symbol of this Fascist state at that time, and Tito did everything to do away with. It was also interesting that Tito, under the formula of "bratstvo i jedinstvo," brotherhood and unity, tried to suppress these national feelings and he did not criticise the Croats in general for having been Fascists. I mean, he himself was a Croat with a Slovene mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've already alluded to this, but you're one of the very few people who may be in a position to give an objective answer to this question. But how would Serbs have perceived the resuscitation of this symbol by Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very negatively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did Tudjman attempt to require that symbol to be adopted even in areas where there was a large Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he tried to have new police uniforms with a swastika on the arm and that Knin was asked to wear these uniforms, which Milan Martic was not prepared to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, at line 14 you used the word "swastika," I assume that you mean chequer-board symbol?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Sorry. Chequer-board symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say Serbs would have viewed that very negatively. Could you elaborate? What would they have, based on your knowledge of the NDH regime, what would they have feared or believed?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NDH was one big horror for the Serbs, and with the independence of Croatia, the symbols of this state reappeared partly. One is this chequer-board symbol. Then there was the units of a party militia by one certain Paraga who used uniforms that were very close to the Ustasha uniforms, and after what had happened 50 years before, the Serbs certainly had to be very concerned about what might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When did that Paraga militia come into existence?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from the early 1990s. Later, I think there was a -- was a split within the Croatian camp and they suppressed it. I think the first were called HOS. HOS, Hrvatske Obrambene Snage, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to some documents that you were shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 448, which is Prosecution tab 5. It has a long P number, it has been exhibited, but 65 ter numbers are sometimes easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this, Ambassador Ahrens, is the document reflecting the Carrington draft convention. Perhaps we can turn to page 2. Now, first of all, it say there that it's -- on the page, it's -- it's the so-called Carrington draft convention. Do you know whether this text, as such, was ever adopted?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not adopted by the conference because Milosevic objected to it. But it was, in a way, adopted by the EC foreign ministers when they made the observance of chapter 2 of that document a precondition for the recognition of the Yugoslav republics independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what it says here, and I'm going to read 1.1(e), with the preamble included, and this is what it says: "The arrangements for a general settlement of the Yugoslav crisis will comprise the following components: "(e) in the framework of a general settlement, recognition of the independence, within ... existing borders, unless otherwise agreed, of those republics wishing it." Now yesterday when this was read you to the words "unless otherwise agreed" were not drawn to your attention. I want to ask you, those words, "unless otherwise agreed," what do they mean to you? What did you understand them to mean at the time?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this was still a proposal, and when you look at this article, you will see that it has certain mutually exclusive possibilities, either confederation, federation or total independence. The one paragraph that we -- refers to the borders -- I mean, I think it has never totally been excluded by the international community that borders may be changed by mutual agreement, but there was, of course, almost a hysteria against the change of borders because at that time everyone was looking at the Soviet Union and not at Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And those first words at the beginning of subpart (e), "in the framework of a general settlement," did you understand those words to mean that a precondition of the creation of states on the territories of the republics was a general settlement for the entire Yugoslav problem?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the idea of the general settlement was such that the Dutch foreign minister, van den Broek, had the ambition of closing the conference until Christmas and the final settlement should come before the end of the year 1991. And this is the idea here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. But leaving aside time -- timing, isn't the point here that a precondition for allowing the republics to establish states on the territories of the republics is a general settlement of the entire Yugoslav question?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not the policy of the EC at the time, and I would not interpret this in that way. But, as we said before, this has never been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D713, please, which is Defence tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, here, on the front page, this appears to be a letter from the permanent representatives of Belgium, France, and the United Kingdom to the president of the the Security Council. And there's attached a declaration on Yugoslavia adopted by the European community on the 8th of November, 1991. If we could please turn the page, there's an annex and it says: "Declaration on Yugoslavia. Extraordinary EPC ministerial meeting." What does EPC stand for?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: European political corporation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The fourth paragraph down: "In this respect, they recall that the prospect of recognition of the independence of those republics wishing it can only be envisaged in the framework of an overall settlement that includes adequate guarantees for the protection of human rights and rights of national or ethnic groups. They urge parties concerned to prepare forthwith legal provisions to this end." Now does that remind you that the position of the EC at this stage, at least on this date, was that a condition of recognition was an overall settlement of the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a condition because if you make an overall settlement a condition, then one party alone could actually prevent any further development. And that is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D95. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have L2, please, which is Defence tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this, Your Excellency, is the resolution to which is attached the Vance Plan. And -- excuse me, it's actually the report to which is attached the Vance Plan. And if we turn to page 8 in e-court, we see the words, again, that we just saw in the declaration. Paragraph 25, about halfway down. And, by the way, this is dated the 11th of December, so this would be a matter of a month after the declaration we were just looking at. And it says, midway through paragraph 25: "The conference" - and this is referring to the conference on Yugoslav, the Carrington conference - "it will recalled is guided by a number of considerations, including those set forth in the declaration issued by the 12 member states of the European community at Rome on 8 November 1991." It then repeats those words. "The conference has also, with the agreement of its participants, ruled out any changes in external or internal borders by means of force. I believe that any selective, uncoordinated departure from those principles could hold very serious dangers not only for the republics of Yugoslavia but for all of her peoples and, indeed, for the maintenance of peace and security in the region." Now I just have this question for you. Do you remember that the words "selective and uncoordinated" were ever used to describe the worst-case scenario for the secession of republics from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And whether you remember that or not, do you read this provision as stating, quite clearly, that there ought to be no further unilateral declarations of independence from Yugoslavia barring a negotiated settlement?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is the 11th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this is a letter by three Ambassadors of three EC members. The same EC, five days later, adopted a declaration by which it laid down the principles for the recognition of newly independent states. And there was one declaration for Yugoslavia, the other one for the Soviet Union and similar cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ambassador, just to be clear, this document in front of us right now, this is the report of the Secretary-General, to which is attached the Vance Plan. The previous document was a cover letter from three representatives on the Security Council attaching the ministerial declaration. So just to clarify -- and I know that you just gave an answer in which you referred to three representatives. Do you want to change your answer at all now that I've drawn this to your attention?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I do not see why we should hear -- discuss the merits of recognition or not. There's a lot of arguments, particularly that you could not do anything in Croatia against what was happening there, as long as this was an internal matter of the state called Yugoslavia that did not exist anymore. And the EC countries decided clearly on the 16th of December, all of them, to recognise republics. I think I should not go beyond this because I myself was not involved in this. I was a member of the Carrington conference. My boss was Carrington. And I was loyal to the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I read in these texts, the few documents that you showed, that this is about recognition of states by other states. And in your questions, you seem to take that as being the same as declaration of independence by republics. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's -- that's a fair distinction, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ambassador, I should have been more precise that what this report is saying, it's not prohibiting unilateral declarations of independence but it does seem to be setting out a policy in terms of recognitions of declarations of independence. Would you care to add anything to your previous answers? I just want to give you a full opportunity to answer my question. Now that I have made the correction.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five days after this document, the EC, all members of the EC, made this declaration on recognition of the independence, and there were very important reasons why they did so, not because anyone liked Yugoslavia to disintegrate. Not one of the EC countries was happy about this. But the situation was such that they saw the necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And now, please, if we could turn to page 11. This takes us into the Vance Plan itself, and the language carries over, or at least there's a reference back to this notion of a comprehensive settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And paragraph 8 says, in defining the UN-protected areas: "The UNPAs would be areas in Croatia in which the Secretary-General judged that special arrangements were required during an interim period to ensure that a lasting cease-fire was maintained ... "As already stated, the special arrangements in these areas would be of an interim nature and would not prejudge the outcome of political negotiations for a comprehensive settlement of the Yugoslav crisis." Am I right in saying -- let's not discuss the precise meaning to you or I of those words. Were those words understood by the Serb side as offering a guarantee or as meaning that the protected area, the final status of the protected areas was not prejudged in the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those lines was meant to define the responsibilities of the conference on one side, which was still the Carrington conference, and the UNPROFOR to be deployed on the other. So they should create the conditions under which the conference would then negotiate the final settlement. That is the real background of this article. It is true that it seems that most of the Serbs believed, indeed, that this opened the possibility for, in the settlement, independently of so far defined principles, and this was the tragic error which I think was also promoted to a certain extent by Western mediators who wanted the Serbs to sign the Vance Plan, while at the same time Genscher was asked to pressure Tudjman to sign it because he also didn't want to sign it. And then in the end it was signed, and I would rather think, and I say that in my book, that some of the Serbs believed that this opened all possibilities. But that was not the the sense of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you say "Western mediators," to whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marrack Goulding. He was the under-secretary general of the United Nations in charge of peacekeeping operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present then, but this is what I assume. I don't know in how far Vance and Okun went along those lines. This does not mean that there was a deliberate undercutting of agreed principles, but I think it is also a little bit in the heat of battle of having this adopted that the Serbians said, Well, this does not preclude anything if you sign this. It's just a preliminary regulation of conditions in place. Sorry, I think I'm still talking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me take you, if I may, to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is 06476; Prosecution tab 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we please could turn, I hope, to e-court page 65, which is your answer to 12(a).

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At least in English, it's page 65 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is German version here. There's another subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think it's now coming up on the page in front of you. Now, the second-last sentence on this page reads: "Unfortunately, ambiguous statements were made by Vance, Okun, and Goulding in connection with the acceptance of the Vance Plan, which the Serbs interpreted as meaning there might very well be border changes in their favour."

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is more or less what I've just said. The word "ambiguous" is a little bit too strong for the translation. It was not deliberately ambiguous but just it could be understood in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what they let it be understood was somehow related to border changes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was only related to them assuming that a solution outside of Croatia was possible. The word "border changes" was really a no word in those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did they let it be known that that issue, did they let it be known to the Serbs, to their Serb interlocutors, that that issue would be a matter for negotiation?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I didn't go that far. First of all, I know Secretary Vance and Okun very well. They would never double-play these things. And I think the explanations which they gave of a more general nature so that the Serbs understood them in a wrong way. As to Marrack Goulding, I don't know. I have not met him personally but I have read his book, which is called The Warmonger, where he has very positive assessments of Milosevic and his like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And from that you infer what?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would at least say that the Serbs would weigh his words, particularly as being particularly important because he was, in the UN, the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Changing gears, Mr. Ambassador, that you met Goran Hadzic for the first time on the 6th of September, 1991, and that the purpose of your visit was: "To get to the signature of Mr. Hadzic under an agreement that should make an existing cease-fire operational and this was on the eve of the Carrington conference." That's at page 7674 for my friend.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Whose idea was it to seek out Mr. Hadzic's signature?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who told Ambassador Wijnaendts whom to see, but it was, of course, clear that, at that time, in that area, Mr. Hadzic was the person that the Serbs considered as being officially in charge. But I do not know, because I was not, myself, involved in these negotiations. Here, I was only a technical advisor. I was -- I was picked up in Zagreb and joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say the Serbs considered that he was the person being officially in charge. First of all, which Serbs are you referring to; and, secondly, in charge of what?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs that had to be talked to, that means the power holders in this -- what later became Sector East. And in charge of what means the leader of these Serbs. The one who could actually decide whether they would observe a cease-fire or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you implying that he has some kind of command and control over armed forces there?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't imply that. I know that Mr. Hadzic does not have a military background. But, I mean, we have a lot of civil presidents in the world who are actually the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge or understanding about the relative authority of Mr. Hadzic versus the JNA commanders who were present in the territory that would later become Sector East?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D702, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you, Mr. Ambassador, used very specific language when you described what you were seeking from Mr. Hadzic. And you said that you were seeking to make an existing cease-fire operational. Now, this in front of us is a cease-fire agreement from the 1st of September, 1991. Was this the cease-fire agreement that you and Mr. Wijnaendts wished to operationalise?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't wish to operationalise a cease-fire because I was not involved. I was a member of the ECMM that at that time had just began executing a mandate regarding these areas. I think it was a cease-fire of the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could please turn the page and go down to the bottom. I'm interested in focussing on the signatories of this cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's done at Belgrade on September 1, 1991, in ten copies. Hans van den Broek of the EC and its member states. Stipe Mesic, president of the SFRY Presidency, and in his capacity as collective Supreme Commander of the armed forces. Ante Markovic, Federal Executive Council president. Alija Izetbegovic, president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency. Momir Bulatovic from Montenegro. Tudjman from Croatia. Kucan from Slovenia. And Milosevic from Serbia. Now it's correct that what we have -- seem to have here is all of the presidents of the republics, plus representatives of the SFRY. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the participants of the conference that was to take place a week later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And some of these leaders, for example, Milan Kucan, had no soldiers involved in ongoing conflicts at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there had been fighting in Slovenia and I think these signatures of these papers wanted to make sure that it would not re-start in Slovenia either. Because the Slovenes had some rumours about certain -- something like cycle or manoeuvre to be planned against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there any connection between the fact that the Carrington conference was to start the next day and the fact that you were seeking Mr. Hadzic's signature?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what Ambassador Wijnaendts told me, that he wanted to get a cease-fire in place when the conference started. Because Lord Carrington, who was to be the chairman of the conference, said he could only negotiate a peace or overall settlement when there was no fighting on the ground. And Carrington said very often, It is not my task to create or to negotiate a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in addition to that, was it, so to speak, the price of admission to being present at the Carrington conference to have signed up to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see in that way. I mean, those who were there were the presidents of the six republics and what we used to call the federals. That means a large part of those fighting on the ground were not there, and exactly for this reason, Wijnaendts sought out those who were in power locally. First, Mr. Hadzic and then Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, then, was it the price of admission for those who were not in de jure positions of authority to be admitted to the Carrington conference?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because they were not admitted to the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But they subsequently did have talks with you and others in the framework of the Carrington conference, did they not?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the talks I attended with them were in Paris, in the Dutch embassy, that had a reason. Later I understand that Wijnaendts and the two vice-presidents of the initial phase of the conference met here in The Hague but I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Hadzic was asked to sign any previous cease-fire agreements or any subsequent cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D96. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, just for the record, that's 1D702 again. Could we have P1345.1325, which is 65 ter 861; Defence tab 6. And we please could go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is the accord implementing the cease-fire agreement of 23 November 1991, the byline is Sarajevo, 2 January 1992. And this is the cease-fire that takes hold and carries through the -- at least in some form, the Vance -- implementation of the Vance Plan. Down there at the bottom, we see that it's signed by A. Raseta Colonel General JNA --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Andrija Raseta, he was the commander in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- Susak, the Defence Minister of Republic of Croatia. And then if we go over the page, it's witnessed by Mr. Vance. Now, does that remind you that this cease-fire, but also other cease-fires, were, in fact, signed by JNA commanders when they pertained to matters in what would become the protected areas in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was heavily involved. They were the one side in the fights in Slovenia. And, as I described yesterday, I myself have seen their tanks and guns dug in around Vukovar and Osijek and shooting into these cities, so they were an important part of the war effort of the Serbs against the Croats. So it is only natural that they had to sign. And if I may say that clearly, Andrija Raseta was a JNA officer so he was the Serb side of that. I know him quite well because we were in the negotiations between the Slovenes and the JNA on the withdrawal of the JNA later. And he was a very nervous person, a Serb from Croatia, who was said that he also -- his family had suffered from the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And after you left Borovo Selo on the 6th of September, am I correct that you crossed over the border into Vojvodina and boarded a helicopter and flew from there towards, first, Osijek, landed, found that the person that you were intending to meet there was not present, and then you flew on from Osijek to Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during the journey between Osijek and Zagreb, am I correct that your helicopter came under anti-aircraft fire?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two ECMM helicopters, Alouette helicopters, very small, white colour, and we came, indeed, under heavy anti-aircraft fire which was clearly aimed at shooting us down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When that happened were you flying over Croat-held territory?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was on the ground. It was over the Papuk mountain in Croatia. I later heard this was Croat-held territory but I don't know whether that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You're fluent in Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What words would you used in Serbo-Croat for police?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed the day before yesterday. This is a sematic question. In some areas it was policija, in others was milicija, but always in the singular. For example, when you take the English word "militia," the singular has a different meaning than the plural. If I talk about the militia of Ruritania, I would think of the police of that -- of that country. But if I talk about the militia -- the militias of Ruritania or, even worse, the militias in Ruritania, then I would think of paramilitary groups or even a gangsterism. And that's what we had in Yugoslavia in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what word would you use in Serbo-Croat and I do apologise to the -- for the transcript. What word would you use in Serbo-Croat for militia, the English word "militia"?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken] which is something like paramilitary group. I don't know. You have people who are more fluent in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I -- looking at the transcript, and I know it's an issue of some significance, perhaps if we could just take a moment and ask if the witness could perhaps spell the word he has just given us or whether he could double-check what's just been put into the transcript, militia versus milicija, so that what he is saying is accurately reflected to avoid any confusion later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me just start perhaps by asking this question: Is there -- is there an exact translation in Serbo-Croat for the word "militia"?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not a linguist in the sense of, let's say, the origin of these words but since I don't know any English-speaking country where the police is called "militia," the Serbian word "milicija" should, at least not always, be translated into English as "militia" but very often as "police," if you go from the function.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And given the fact that the -- and we'll come back to the spelling at the end, given the fact that the Serbian word "milicija" sounds very similar to the English word "militia," for English speakers or for people who are writing in English there is a danger of confusion of those two concepts, is there not?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, that is the use of the singular or the plural. I think when you say, in German, for example, "die Miliz" of such and such, I would still think it is the police of that area. But when I say "Milizen," which is militias, I would certainly think of rather unsavory groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But it is also possible that if someone says, "I am milicija," that could be written down in English, mistakenly, as "militia," assuming that those two are synonyms. Right?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, in Serbo-Croatian there's a word "milicioner" which is the individual participating in a militia. That is a policeman. And if I had to translate to Serbo-Croatian into English I would translate with "policeman."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now perhaps we could take up the Prosecutor's suggestion and earlier you gave us a definition of the word "militia" in Serbo-Croat. Would you mind spelling the word you used?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, milicija is m-i-l-i-c-i-j-a. And when I said militias, I would translate -- I may have a better translation like paravojne, which means paramilitary, p-a-r-a-v-o-j-n-e, and then I would jedinice, which means units, "jedinice." Paravojne Jedinice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you a few questions about the implementation of the Vance Plan and you've discussed --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- to a fair extent during your examination-in-chief about the Vance Plan. Can you tell us your view as to whether, under the Vance Plan, whether UNPROFOR was obliged to use force, if necessary, to defend the protected areas from Croatian attack?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what the mandate says. I mean, not that is what the mandate says but one has to look into the mandate as to that. It is not a chapter 7 mandate but they could, of course, defend themselves. And since in the attack in January 1993, I think two or three French soldiers died, they could have shot back in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So if fair to say that the only way in which UNPROFOR forces would be -- would find themselves in a situation where they are obliged and able under the chapter 6 mandate to use force to protect the protected areas, is if they are physically on the lines, on the borders of the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was another point of contention between the two sides because the Serbs, indeed, wanted UNPROFOR only to be on the line of confrontation and not inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment. But I just want to focus on an initial or preliminary question first. And that is, consistent with self-protection, isn't it right that the only occasion that UNPROFOR is going to use force to defend the protected areas is if UNPROFOR forces are on the edge of the protected areas and in harm's way of any Croat attack?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about protecting the United Nations protected areas only but about protecting themselves, and in so far, they could use force. But there were not to withstand an overall attack, which they could not. They were not strong enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have P2882, please; Prosecution tab 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that you did look at yesterday. It's from the RSK Ministry of Interior dated the 30th of April, 1992. The subject is conversations between EU representatives and the RSK president. It's addressed to the state committee for co-operation with the UN, B. Jovic personally; the SDB of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, to J. Stanisic personally; to the SSNO security administration,

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasiljevic personally. Before we get into the content, any idea why these individuals are being -- would be addressed on a letter of this sort which incidentally is prepared and signed by Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the contents of the letter? Because before I can say whether the addressees are right, I have to know what's in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's dive in then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, by the way, this document ostensibly recounts a conversation of the 29th of April, 1992, between Goran Hadzic and the deputies of Lord Carrington, Thierry De Beauce and Wijnaendts, and someone named Guy Yelda, assistant of Mr. Beauce.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually the deputy at that time was only Monsieur Thierry De Beauce, French minister of state. The organise head of the conference was Ambassador Wijnaendts. And Guy Yelda, G-u-y Y-e-l-d-a, was the French assistant from Mitterrand's office for De Beauce.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Second paragraph down: "Hadzic evaluated that the loss of lives on a daily basis was caused also by an inadequate disposition of the UNPROFOR forces which were deployed about 20 to 30 kilometres behind the line of the front, leaving, in that way, the Serbian population in the borderland areas towards Croatia." Now, based on what you know, is that descriptively correct that UNPROFOR forces were well inside the boundaries of the previous confrontation lines?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was myself not dealing with the deployment of the UNPROFOR forces. What I do remember is that the Serbs wanted them on the line of confrontation, and the Croats and the international community wanted them all over the UNPAs, and that was unfortunately necessary because some very unpleasant things were going on inside the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you know -- and I understand you're not intimately familiar with the situation on the ground, but based on what you did know, reports you did read, did you know that the areas on -- around the confrontation lines were unstable, insecure?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was such that around the end of 1991, beginning of 1992, there was a real standoff and there was a cease-fire that held. As I said yesterday, President Tudjman wanted to prevent under all circumstances a Cyprus situation to arise and that is why the Croats became offensive here and there. The first such incursion was a place called the Miljevacki Plateau, the second was this serious one which is the object of 802. There were others, the worst was in the Medak pocket where Croats committed very bad crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So just to give a global view of the situation, it's right, isn't it, that after the creation of the protected areas, the Serbs were content with the status quo, whereas the Croats were pressuring to restore these territories to their control?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, this is a correct statement. The Croat -- the Serbs, of course, in what they consider their areas continued ethnic cleansing. Whereas Tudjman, who did not want to lose these territories, felt that he could not allow the situation to become permanent as in Cyprus. This was the situation. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And we'll get to the ethnic cleansing piece of this. But, for the time being, isn't it right that the areas around - and I'm not sure I got an answer to this question - the areas around the confrontation lines, including the pink zones, were unstable and dangerous places?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a natural fact, yes. I crossed them often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can look at the last paragraph on this page: "Colonel Stojan Spanovic, the RSK minister of defence, pointed out that they had information that the RH Main Staff planned the operations for forcefully seizing the RSK territory which was not under the UNPROFOR protection. Therefore, we doubt that the inadequate establishing of the UNPROFOR units is a sort of pressure on RSK in the conditions of changed circumstances and relations in SFRY since the time when Vance's plan and the peace concept were accepted." Now this document is the 30th of April. How long after this did the Miljevacki Plateau attack take place?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I can look it up in the book, I have it here, but I can't say it out of my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, is there any truth at all to Spanovic's suspicion here that UNPROFOR is deploying in such a way to put pressure on the Serbs out of a fear that an attack by the Croats would be successful and the territory would be taken?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is what Mr. Spanovic thinks. I think it's not correct. You have to see that this is the document set up by the Carrington conference, and on the other side is the deployment of UNPROFOR. These are at that time still two totally different institutions because only ICFY was a largely UN enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if I understand correctly, your information about human rights violations in the protected areas came mainly, if not exclusively, from ECMM reports and then we have the one document from the Czech Ambassador. Would those be the sources of your information about human rights abuses in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I had a contact with Widows of Vukovar and with other Croatian individuals who had fled the areas. I had this impression of the prisoners on the 6th of September. We saw the almost systematic destruction of houses and churches of the other side in the areas. Then there was a large number of real furious reports and -- both oral and written reports of ECMM observers. Then there were -- there was information by the Croatian government which was to a large extent rather reliable. Tudjman makes these points in one of his letters to the United Nations. So there was quite a lot, but, of course, those who perpetrated human rights abuses would be well advised not to do so before the eyes of international observers although even that happened. I read in reports that ethnic cleansing went on under the eyes of UNPROFOR soldiers. And Ilok was in a daylight operation where both UNPROFOR and the ECMM were involved, so there was no doubt about these human rights violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The Ilok event occurred in October 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That was before the creation of the protected areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the ECMM was in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the information from the Widows of Vukovar, that pertained to crimes that occurred in November 1991, is that correct, around the time of the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know because I don't know who the individuals were behind these names, but it would certainly refer to the times between something like April and November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So some of the information that you've just been describing, that concerned crimes that occurred in 1991 and early 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, if I have mentioned UNPROFOR in that regard, that's an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever observe or learn or perceive or were told that there was any decline in the incidents of human rights abuses over time and, in particular, after the institution of the protected areas.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the worst happened in 1991 when these areas were conquered, but that is why I was slightly surprised that UNPROFOR reported that ethnic cleansing went on under their eyes because the fighting proper had stopped. I mean, there was the cease-fire and there were these Croatian incursions, but the situation in 1991 was totally different. And one has also to see that ethnic cleansing was almost not necessary in areas where the Serbs were, as in Knin, 87 per cent, but in areas where the Serbs are only 37 per cent, as in Vukovar, you have to cleanse out if you want to make a clean shop - sorry for these expressions - quite large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what you just said ... well, strike that preamble. Is it the case that by the time the protected areas are set up and in particular in Sector East, the vast majority of non-Serbs have already left, either to flee the fighting or they've been forced out or by whatever other reason?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge of this, but the figures of expelled or -- expelled Croats or refugees that Tudjman gave in those times were rather high.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you yourself raised the issue of human rights abuses with Mr. Hadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That was during your meeting with Mr. Hadzic on the 23rd of September, 1991, in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did that at many occasions because I was head of the Working Group in charge of minorities, and the Krajina Serbs never disputed that I was in charge of non-Serbs living in their area. So I had a right to -- to raise these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's have your statement again, 06476.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could start, please, with e-court page 14. Now, it's the answer to question 20, so perhaps if we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, there is a reference -- you're being asked about the meeting of 23rd of September, 1992, with Goran Hadzic: "Where was the meeting held?" Go over the page, please. In ... well, it did say in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then if we go down, please, to the answer to subpart (f): "Do you recall any other occasions in which the issues of ethnic cleansing or human rights violations were raised in the presence of Hadzic? If so, please provide details. Answer -- we see the German, "Nein." If we go over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, just for the record I want to make sure that we have this on the screen in English.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this "no" means that I have not heard these points being taken up with Mr. Hadzic by anyone else. The instances in which I talked with Mr. Hadzic on these points were, of course, anyway in this paper and they are, well, more or less exhaustively there, but the issue that was my proper mandate of looking after non-Serbs in the RSK came, of course, up when I met with the leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the participants in your Working Group were only the representatives of the republics; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right for the Carrington conference. Later, during the ICFY, we hardly had anymore such plenary sessions because they led nowhere. We were dealing with individual republics and we tried to go in the direction of what we called the trilaterals, the government, a minority and us around the same table. This succeeded in Macedonia but -- and sometimes even in Serbia and Kosovo, but not for some time in Croatia. In Voganes [phoen] that was the trilateral.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you saying that the first time that the Serb minority representatives were involved in the context of the Working Group now, in the context of the Working Group, the first such meeting was in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we had meetings, for example, the Paris meeting, but it is correct that particularly after January 1992, Carrington and later, from April, De Beauce, rather dealt themselves with these issues. But the last meeting I had with the Serbs from Krajina under the Carrington conference was in July 1992 in Belgrade and that is in the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So that's different from, separate from, not the same as, the Working Group on minorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depends. When I talked to Hadzic about non-Serbs in the RSK, I have my hat as minorities Working Group chairman. But when we discussed the relationship between Zagreb and Knin, we had these special arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your view is that you raised the issue of human rights abuses with Mr. Hadzic on occasions other than this September 1992 meeting in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, September 1992 meeting in Belgrade was the first meeting after the setting up of the ICFY. I had met Mr. Hadzic in London the month before, and I had had I think, at that time - I would have to check it - my first Plenary Session, may have been the only one, in Geneva. And after that I travelled to Belgrade to have a first contact as the new conference representative with the RSK Serbs and that was when I met Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, is it right that the first time that you could have raised it would have been on the 23rd of September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I could have raised in October 1991. We could have and we should have raised it on the 6th of September, 1991. And actually, Wijnaendts raised it, for example, in Knin, the week thereafter, when he wanted the signature of Babic on the cease-fire and he obtained the release of five prisoners from Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I should have put my question a little bit more precisely, Mr. Ambassador, I'm sorry for that. When I say that you could have, I mean to say the first time that it fell squarely within your mandate to raise it was on the 23rd of September, 1992, during that meeting in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I had the mandate under the Carrington conference as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Except that under the Carrington conference, if I understand correctly, you weren't meeting with Mr. Hadzic in the context of the Working Group, were you?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the Working Group still had these Plenary Sessions which were attended only by representatives of the six republics. And the two Serbian representatives there, Kreca and Avramov, declined to speak about the situation in the Krajina because they said this had nothing to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So with those answers in place, come back to the question I asked before. The first time that it fell within your mandate to raise it with Mr. Hadzic would have been the 23rd of September, 1992, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not within my mandate. Because under my mandate I could have done so, and the circumstances in October 1991, in Paris, were not such that I wanted to do it because we had this discussion about Mr. Babic objecting to my presence in that meeting, and I did not want to put up the other hat but I had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And when you did raise this issue with Mr. Hadzic on the 23rd of September, 1992, in Belgrade, am I right that he acknowledged that such abuses had occurred?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did acknowledge that under conditions of war such -- such events had occurred, yes. Under conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what does that mean? What did he say in respect of the relationship between violence and conditions of war? Sorry, let me correct my question. What did he say about the connection between human rights abuses and the conditions of war?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the answer normally consisted of three points. First point, we have a constitution and laws in our country that guarantees all these rights. Second point, we have a functional judicial system that sees to it that this is being implemented. Third, I do not deny that violations occurred. This is understandable under the conditions of war. I wouldn't know any more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he talk to you at all about the obstacles, given the conditions on the ground, to preventing or remedying human rights abuses?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. I mean, I pondered it, of course. I asked myself what the relationship is with people like Arkan or Frenki. But we did not discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He never said, for example, that a large percentage of the population in Sector East following the war and as a result of the war were armed, including with rifles?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember that he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he ever say that was a problem with demobilising the large number of individuals who were outside of the framework of the special police?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in discussions with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you that the constraints on the regular police under the Vance Plan, namely, only possessing side-arms, also hampered the ability to prevent those crimes or human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not and we actually did not discuss these last three points which you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You didn't seek to press him on how it could be that these violations could occur?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. What we did discuss was the necessities of a protection, so that was more future-oriented than past-oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how would you compare Mr. Hadzic's -- the nature of Mr. Hadzic's reaction to the nature of the reactions that you received from other Serb interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic was much more accessible than most of the others. So, in one instance he asked me for a text of that Croatian law. In another instance he asked me to help with the -- the system of protecting human rights in the RSK. And then in Plitvice, where I think we had the longest and most private conversation because it was just the two of us, he said that he personally could not fully exclude a solution inside of Croatia but that every Serb politician who said that in public would be in danger. That was the widest he went in contacts with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I do see the clock. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Excellency, this is time for our first break. Thirty minutes, same as yesterday. We'll come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Amongst the war conditions that were mentioned by Mr. Hadzic that you mentioned before the break, do you recall that he, amongst those, referred to the large population of displaced persons who were -- Serbs, who were present in certain protected areas, certain parts of the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that he made such a remark to me, but he spoke in public several times about the refugee situation, and also inviting Serbs from other areas of the former Yugoslavia to settle in Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in respect of the -- not from other parts of Yugoslavia but from parts of sector -- excuse me, parts of Croatia that had been seized by Croat forces, there were many Serbs who moved into the protected areas without the need for any advertising; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But there was also some advertising and some pressure. But also on the Croatian side. Even stronger on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know how many houses were destroyed, Serb houses were destroyed in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but it was, according to Mr. Pupovac, who was a Serb active in Zagreb, quite a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were told it was a thousand?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been in that dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did the former residents of those houses know that their houses had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did international mediators, representatives, avoid raising human rights issues with their Serb interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my feeling, I think these points should have been raised much more. Now, of course, Vance and Owen were after a solution for the horrible Bosnian problem and they fully concentrated on the Vance-Owen Peace Plan for Bosnia where there was, of course, also a part on human rights, but generally they dealt with the big political problems without going into these details. Whereas I considered, if I may say it with my words, my main task to deal with the poor victims of that ethnic madness that had befallen Yugoslavia. Of all nations: Croats, Serbs, Albanians, what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor asked you yesterday whether you knew whether Mr. Hadzic had taken any steps to try to remedy the situation as you reported it to him. Were you in any position to know what steps he may have taken, whether he took such steps?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could imagine that he might have told me if he had taken such steps because this would take some of the problem away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ask him on any subsequent occasion whether he had taken such steps?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you think that, after this September meeting in Belgrade, do you now recall or do you not recall whether you, again, raised the issue of human rights violations with Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, we certainly discussed these points also in Plitvice where we had a long discussion and talked about everything that was of concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Aside from the list from the Widows of Vukovar, did you address the human rights situation with him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure I did but I do not recall in concrete terms because we also discussed the overall situation, as I mentioned before the break, the solution for the problem in the Krajina where he, for once, said that he would not totally exclude the solution inside of Croatia. Had he prevailed, the Serbs would still be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have D73, please; Defence tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is a crypto cable from -- under the name of Nambiar with the signature Cedric Thornberry to Goulding dated 30 November 1992. Subject: Discussions with Knin authorities. Do you remember whether you saw this document at the time or have you seen it recently?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could please turn the page. Under paragraph 6 -- and there's no indication incidentally that Mr. Hadzic is present. It's a conversation with Stojan Spanovic and then with the minister of energy of the time, Bjegovic.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I read this first? You refer to number 6, yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm coming to 6. I just wanted to give you that information from page 1.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Spanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then now --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and Bjegovic, who was the prime minister of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is before Bjegovic apparently becomes -- perhaps we should go back to page 1, just to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked not to overlap because it is impossible to interpret what they are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Understood. So there we see that it appears there's a discussion with Stojan Spanovic, minister of defence of the time, and Bjegovic, minister of energy of the time. Could we go to page two, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "We kept clear of displaced persons' issues on this occasion, and said little about disarmament. But Spanovic volunteered that they were making a very big effort to clean up their act by arresting their bandits and making life hot for their gangsters (especially in Sector East). Clearly very sensitive to this matter, now, he agreed precisely with our analysis and felt the 'decline into anarchy' line we have been publicly taking could destroy any residual credibility they may have." And the question I have for you is this: Did you observe that Mr. Hadzic in his discussions with you was concerned about any loss of credibility arising from allegations of human rights abuses in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any remark by Mr. Hadzic comparable to what we have here in number 6 by Spanovic. He might have made it, but I think I would have recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: In the last sentence reads: "Colleagues confirm that they are indeed attempting to crack down on at least some of their thugs, and that the serious crime rate has dropped appreciably." Now, do you recall - and the date of this again is the end of November 1992 - do you recall whether there were any reports indicating that the crime rate, in particular in Sector East, dropped appreciably around or before this time?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. And I remember, for example, when we drove to Sector East, that the Belgian troops that were there showed us at several instances jeeps that had been stolen from them and then repainted. And when I asked them, Why didn't you take it back, they said, They are so poor. And I remember that Mr. Thornberry, whenever he had to see local authorities somewhere in the Krajina, he said, We are going to see the local bandit. So this went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The crime is being perpetrated against UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that one was against UNPROFOR, yeah. They stole their jeeps. But that was a sign of the general lawlessness, that they even dare take these jeeps. I didn't hear that they took the Russians' jeeps but the Belgians'.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you speak Russian?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
