utterances.text: The confusion we discussed earlier -- or not confusion, the distinctions, the language about milicija, militia, does that confusion arise in the Russian language?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And my Russian is not as good as my Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you testified at pages 7741 to 42 about handing a list between 50 and 150 names --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- that had been drawn up by a group called the Widows of Vukovar. You gave this list to Mr. Hadzic and he looked at it and said they were all dead. And you said, and I quote, and this is on 7742: "We did not discuss who had killed them, for what reasons they were dead or so, he just said that this was the state of affairs." Just a couple of follow-up questions about this --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just correct. Mr. Hadzic did not say, This is the state of affairs, but I wanted to say that we just discussed the state of affairs but not the causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he said he recognised any of the names as being people he knew personally?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not say that. He looked at the list very carefully and from this I would conclude that he knew who were the persons on the list. Otherwise he could not tell me that they were all dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he say whether he knew the manner in which they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he indicate whether he believed they had been killed in combat --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, I just wanted to finish my question. Did he say whether he believed they had been killed in combat or whether they had been killed in some other circumstance?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not. I mean, when such points were brought with Serbs of the RSK, the normal excuse was that they had been killed in combat. But at this occasion, Mr. Hadzic said nothing to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you can't say in this case whether that was an excuse or not in relation to these names, can you?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know who the people were. I mean, the point that the group called itself the Widows of Vukovar somehow would logically make me deduct that they knew that they were dead. Because I'm a widow when my husband doesn't live anymore. But I think one should not go into such semantic exercise. It was just women who were very much concerned about what had become of their husbands and sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would like, if I may, to ask you some questions about the so-called Resolution 802 negotiations following the incursion by Croat forces in the area of Maslenica bridge, and you spoke about that during your testimony and I'll try not to ask you to repeat too much of what you've already said. But let me just first ask you: Is it your general impression that Mr. Hadzic was the deciding negotiator or interlocutor in relation to these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly in the meetings which we had in conference rooms in New York and Geneva. But as I may have said, I don't know whom he had to consult before he made a decision or whether he had to consult anyone. But among these RSK representatives who were there with him, such as Paspalj and the foreign minister, he was clearly number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did the fact that Mr. Hadzic was from Sector East have anything at all to do with your understanding or perception of his authority in relation to these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I said somewhere that, of course, he was not so directly involved because he was from Sector East which is far away from the theatre of this 802 operation and in so far he might not have been so directly interested in what it is. On the other hand, he was, from February 1992 onwards, the president of the entire RSK and, as such, he had to deal with it. Otherwise, Babic would anyway have been the one to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 06476, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Which is your statement again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe we're looking for e-court page 21, the answer to question 22(g). Yes, that does look like the right page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you make it bigger?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the bottom paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Hadzic was the head of the Serbian negotiating delegation by virtue of his position. But in two ways he was not really involved. For one thing, he was from the UNPA Sector East, which was far away from the Maslenica bridge. Then he also did not have any military background, even though he occasionally wore a Serbian paramilitary uniform." And these negotiations are going on in 1993, March onwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it started in February but I would have to check. And February, well, he had been president of the RSK for one year at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's what I am very interested in in your answer and I'm curious about. Because on the one hand, he is, as you know, as of this date the president of the RSK, but here you are saying because he is from the UNPA Sector East, which was far away from the Maslenica bridge, he was not really involved. I'm curious if you can help us understand why you say that, or said that.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only repeat. Because this did not concern him so directly because he was from an area far away from the theatre of these operations. And the second point is that he, indeed, seems not to have had a military background. He might have fulfilled his obligation as a soldier in Yugoslavia. They had a draft. But, otherwise he was not a military officer so...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet we see in the documents that he is present at many of the negotiations. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And he is the head of the delegations to those negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet here you are saying he is not really involved. How are those two reconcilable?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be better to replace "involved" by "deeply interested." Of course, he was involved, he was head of the delegation, but his personal interest might have been less intense than that of Babic or Martic who were from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were Martic and Babic the ones making the final -- I don't want to say final. Were they the ones determining the negotiating strategy?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Babic had been sidelined a year before. He might have been mayor of Knin at that time, I don't remember. He still played a role but he was clearly not in the political mainstream, and Martic had still to come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Hadzic isn't so interested, then what personality, which person was interested? Which person was primarily concerned with this issue?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, in a way, this concerned, of course, also the overall situation of the RSK towards Croatia and in so far Mr. Hadzic was interested. But on the other hand, the area we dealt with and these details and niceties of these 802 negotiations had to do with the territory to the south of Knin and almost on the Adriatic Sea, so that was a totally different theatre. He might not have known the villages, whereas the others knew them. But I don't think that the Knin, in opposition to the overall leadership, had the decisive influence. Hadzic was in -- in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, why we have this document in front of us, let's turn, please, to e-court page 24. I'm looking to the answer under subpart (e) which, just to give you the context, this is -- the question that you're originally asked concerns the negotiations in Norway in 1993. And then there's a subquestion that says: "What economic arguments did you make to convince Hadzic and the RSK government to reach an agreement? How did Hadzic and the Serb leaders respond to these arguments?" "Hadzic showed little interest in economic matters. His home, Sector East, which directly bordered with Serbia, did not need any Croatian concessions. It was totally different in Sector South, which was cut off from the coast." It's also true, isn't it, that Sector South is cut off from Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you enlighten us as to -- or expand on this answer, in what sense is there, are there, would there be, divergent interests in respect of these two sectors?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Knin was a very important railway centre in former Yugoslavia. Since the railways did not run anymore, a high percentage of the workers in Knin was jobless. Knin and the areas above the coast, I mean, these Serb majority areas, were not directly on the coast but very close to it. And many of these Serbs, I think, had employment in the coast and drew their income from there. So this fell flat. And when you looked at the landscape around Knin it's a barren country. It is all stone and -- and little even forests or so. So they were in a very bad situation, and they needed fertiliser, they needed a lot of basic stuff to run their economy. And, since on the other side there was Bosnia and there were parts of Bosnia which were not Serb-populated but Croatian or Muslim populated, so hostile to them, this was a very difficult situation. And we had hoped that the situation would make them make concessions because they simply had to, but the national feelings were much, much stronger than the understanding of economic matters with most of the leaders of the former Yugoslavia across the board. Now in Sector East where there were oil wells which were refined close to Belgrade and where there was a wealthier agriculture, although, of course, with the loss of a high percentage of the population, this was also in a mess, but these were different problems. And Sector East did not need the Croats. Sector South and Sector North needed them. And the Croats, on their side, also needed Serbian concessions because the railway line. Then electricity lines. And the -- the dam in Peruca. All of this had been necessary for -- for -- for example, the well-being of the Croatian and Dalmatian coast, which was the basis of tourism.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did the joblessness and the very difficult situation in Sector South have any impact on politics in the Krajina region? By "Krajina region" I mean Sector South and Sector North.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the political wish to establish an independent Serbian state was much stronger than the wish to re-establish the economic links with Croatia which would raise the economic well-being of the area, and in so far I do not see much of an influence of the contacts on the political decisions of the Krajina leadership. Not even those who were from the area, like Babic or Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you observe, based on your contacts with Serb interlocutors, that there was any distinction in the power structures between the Krajina and Sector East? Were these separate power structures or were they all unified under the umbrella of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were all unified under the umbrella of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That didn't answer my question. It's enlightening but ...

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. I think they were unified under the umbrella of the RSK politically. Economically they were different. And the direct influence of Serbia was, of course, much bigger in Sector East which bordered Serbia directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were there separate power brokers in the Krajina region who had effective control over - and I'm asking this very generally - who had control over -- or separate control over decision-making in that area?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The persons we discussed with were always speaking -- or after the RSK was established speaking for the entire RSK and not for different sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But did you become aware at some point surely that there was a schism in the politics of the RSK and that this schism, I suggest, was correlative with the distinction between Krajina and Sector East?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it that way. I mean, the first clear split that occurred was when the Vance Plan had to be accepted. Because Babic definitely did not want to accept the Vance Plan and we interpreted the developments that then came, that Hadzic became president of the entire country and then accepted the Vance Plan, as the work of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's see if we can illuminate this topic by looking at a few documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: First of all, could we have P45, and this relates to the issue of the submission of the agreement, the 802 agreement, to the RSK Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now you were shown this document that is coming up in front us from Wahlgren to Annan and the date is the 22nd of April. And the subject is reported to be parliamentary session of the RSK in Okucani on 20 April 1993. If we turn the page, we see the correspondence that is referred to on the cover page and it's another cover page. And this one is from someone named Jusuf Khalaf OIC Civil Affairs. The name is K-h-a-l-a-f. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the UNPROFOR civil section, which was headed by Thornberry, had field stations and in Sector West it was obviously this person. Whether I have met him, I don't know. There was another one in Sector East -- in Sector South in Knin, which appeared yesterday, Jeannie Peterson, and these -- this personnel changed rather often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says the drafter is Jusuf Khalaf and at the bottom it says: "Message: Please find attached the notes of the above-mentioned session. Any more information will be communicated to you in due course." Now -- well, let's turn to the next page for starters. The title of this page is: Notes on RSK parliament session in Okucani on 20th April 1993. With the possible exception of the first two words, the typeface appears to be different than what we saw on the previous page. Now, given the reference on the cover page to drafter being Jusuf Khalaf, and given what you know about UNPROFOR protocols, could you be sure, looking at this, that Mr. Khalaf is the author of the page in front of us?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, these field stations of UNPROFOR had not only one person and so it might be -- have been written by a colleague. For example, sometimes my papers have SC, which is Sancho Coutinho, which is normally on my dealings. This may explain this change in type here. Another possibility is that the person who was there must have known Serbo-Croatian and it could be the interpreter who has written it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's what I was going to ask you and I know -- I take on board what you said about Mr. Khalaf. I suppose it wouldn't assist you if I asked whether you saw any documents or have any indication at all that Mr. Khalaf spoke Serbo-Croat?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No idea. But normally they did not. I was still a rather rare bird.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm done with that document. Could we please move to 01681; Prosecution tab 24. I'm sorry, I called the wrong number. Could I have 05369, please; Prosecution tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And one more aspect of that last document. It says that the session occurred on the 20th of April, the parliamentary session.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that date accord with your recollection of the date when the agreement was rejected?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, the agreement was rejected on the basis of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember saying in your book - and, for the record, I'll just give the reference, it's page 143 of your book - that it was shot down by the RSK Assembly on 24 April?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: May be an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not saying you're in error. I'm merely drawing your attention to the discrepancy between what you say in your book and this document.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know. But I think, in any case, this does not make a difference in the development that we had had a drawn-out negotiation on an agreement with 22 drafts and that then the one that had finally been accepted was shot down by the Assembly some two weeks afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of this document, which you prepared, it seems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I have written it myself, yeah. But it could also be Coutinho.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the date is 30 April 1993, and you're describing a meeting with Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Misa Milosevic of the same day, 30th of April, 1993. And five lines from the bottom, you say: "Hadzic answered that they wanted the April 6 agreement. When he again requested the presence of Serbian police in the 802 area, I stated categorically that I would not even transmit such a proposal to the Croatian side. He could only accept the agreement as it was and give the co-chairmen of ICFY the assurance provided for in the Annex ..." Next page, please. "... of the agreement. After some discussion, Hadzic distanced himself from part of his Assembly's views and said that he would not seek any changes in the text of the agreement; he would make the statement about his police not entering the 802 area. "If the meeting in Athens was successful on Bosnia. If not, things would be very difficult for him too. After this, we agreed to continue the discussion ... Hadzic added that in case of a positive outcome in Athens, he would be grateful if ICFY or UNPROFOR could give him some assurance about the safety of Serbs against further Croatian attacks and about the structure to be worked out by UNPROFOR for the 802 areas. He needed something that would allow him to justify before his Assembly why he had accepted agreement not endorsed by this Assembly, without any changes." Now, I'm not so interested in the details of the position. But do you recall that during this meeting Mr. Hadzic was reflecting that there was pressure from elements inside that Assembly that were not amenable to allowing him to conclude an agreement?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what do you know about those elements, if anything?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, we -- we know Mile Paspalj, who used to be the Speaker of that parliament and who was a hard-liner, according to what I know. And there was, of course, more such hard-liners in that parliament. I remember, for example, after Dzakula had signed that Daruvar agreement, someone in the Assembly said that Dzakula was a traitor. This sort of people, and I think there were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Hadzic ever tell you that he had been accused of being a traitor as a result of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it was interesting in the report about the session of the parliament that Mr. Hadzic, in two sentences, said more or less in the first sentence the agreement was good. In the second, the agreement was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what do you think that indicates?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he, in fact, would have liked the agreement to go through and be signed, and his concern about the safety of the Serbs in the area where Serb police would not go again, these villages, one of them is Islam Grcki, are understandable and justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just while we have this page in front of us, if we could look at the first sentence of paragraph -- sorry, the second paragraph under item 3: "Hadzic then reiterated that the Krajina Serbs wanted a separate existence from the diaspora Serbs in Croatia." Now does that reflect a common refrain by Mr. Hadzic insisting that the RSK territories would not be reintegrated into Croatia, into the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, when I told Mr. Hadzic, for example, about this constitutional law and our negotiations about it, he would always say, These are Serbs living under Croatian rule, I wish them well, but we are not concerned. This does not have any relation to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you are a Serbo-Croat speaker and you used the expression in English here "a separate existence." Can you indicate to us why you would have used those particular words, "a separate existence"?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no particular reason to use those words. It could also be an independent state or an existence outside of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it possible that that reflects directly the syntax used by Mr. Hadzic with you?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, normally I would not make wordly quotes, and "separate existence" was one of the words which we used for these possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D97. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01681, please; Prosecution tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The last document was the 30th of April. This document is the 14th of June, 1993. It's from Stoltenberg under the signature of Cedric Thornberry to Annan. Subparagraph -- or paragraph 2 -- or the subject line is: Croatian Krajina meetings in Geneva on 16 June. "After the Serb military had failed to turn up at Topusko on 20 May to sign the interim cease-fire, we got messages indicating that they wanted to speak military to military on this matter, no civilians, no politics. After meetings involving FC and CMO, it was confirmed that this was a somewhat fraudulent prospectus as what General Novakovic in fact wanted was to wrest control of the political handling of the implementation of 802 from the designated representatives of RSK in Geneva in favour of himself and those who think like him." Do you remember anything about the incident being described here, or the event?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I have seen that paper, I think, even at the epoch when it was written. Mile Novakovic was the one who actually ended the -- the 802 negotiations proper. I think he was the one who wrote that letter that said that the letter by Stoltenberg and Owen to the Serbs was dirty joke. So this shows a certain split. The military was certainly not satisfied with what the civilian part, in this case the government and Mr. Hadzic, wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do I understand correctly that what General Novakovic is attempting to do is engage in direct negotiations with the Croat side under the auspices of the international mediators; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But not the international mediators -- well, he wanted somehow to also have a role in the ICFY but as normally as a general and a military leader he would deal with UNPROFOR only. But later, for example, in Norway, Novakovic was together with Hadzic in the Serb delegation and Hadzic was the leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly from your last answer that Novakovic was making direct contacts with the officials of the ICFY, without going through Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he discussed this with Hadzic. But this paper shows that Novakovic wanted to turn up in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And according to this, wrest control of the political handling of the implementation of 802.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is something what the author of this paper thinks. I don't see that, and both were together in Norway and I could not see any contradiction between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you didn't observe this --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- wresting of control?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it should be seen, of course, that towards the end of that same year, Mr. Hadzic was slowly -- well, there was these elections in the RSK and he was replaced by Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it possible that Thornberry or Stoltenberg knew things about General Novakovic in relation to these negotiations that you didn't?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. We were in constant contact and Stoltenberg was the chairman of our conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you in contact with Thornberry about these matters?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It goes on: "Thus while talking provisional cease-fire, Novakovic and colleagues have in fact been trying to find a new way to implement 802 which will operate more to their interest." Do you have any idea who is being referred to when it says "Novakovic and colleagues" having some kind of a separate interest or a personal interest or an interest of some kind? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, other Serb military. And these colleagues, I think, this might extend partially into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it a reference to Martic?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would not normally say that Martic is a colleague of Novakovic. Because Martic was a policeman but not a military, in the strict sense. But it could be. I mean, Martic then later was the next president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It goes on: "All those associated with the 6 April agreement are held in suspicion by the RSK military, including President Hadzic, and any mention of Misa" - next page - "Milosevic provokes nasty and dismissive remarks." Now do you remember whether Mr. Hadzic mentioned that the military was pushing back against his stance or his attempt to negotiate an agreement under 802?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not discuss this with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he say that he was being held in suspicion by the RSK military because of his involvement?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The RSK Serbs almost or practically never spoke about their internal splits with us, the foreign mediators. One could hear something from Babic after he was deposed, but not too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during his lakeside discussion with you in Plitvice, did he say what the consequences might be for him, not in relation to the 802 agreement, but if he had ever revealed candidly that his view was that there might be a solution to be found within Croatia for the RSK?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need to say that because it was quite clear to me, and it showed a certain degree of trust by Mr. Hadzic because if I had gone public with what he had told me, I might endangered him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What does that mean, "endangered him"?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they might have arrested him as a traitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender this document, 01681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I'm told that there are a few cables under this document number. Is it your intention to tender them all?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would prefer not to, in principle, so I think if we could just take the front three pages. We can take care of that Mr. President, if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So I understand you will come back to us with the final solution on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: While we still have this on the screen, could we turn the page -- or, no, we can just go down to the bottom of the page, please. "After a prolonged meeting of the Supreme Defence Council this morning, which Bjegovic, Novakovic and Martic attended, we received their agreement to the Geneva meetings, and now have provisional delegations ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me just stop there. Does it appear to you from that that Mr. Hadzic isn't present at that particular Supreme Defence Council meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not -- well, I don't know this. Because when Bjegovic, Novakovic and Martic attended, this does not exclude that the president wasn't in charge. I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Any information at all about why Thornberry or Stoltenberg would only have mentioned those three names and not have mentioned Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because that were the ones they talked to at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what do you know, if anything, about the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very much. Just the body that dealt with military matters on a national -- on a national basis, which means the entire RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether decisions could be taken by the Supreme Defence Council with only the three listed names in attendance?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Milosevic said so, yes. Not Misa Milosevic but Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1686, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is from Coutinho, S. Coutinho to Wahlgren dated 18 June 1993. Again, that's your assistant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can turn over the page, your name appears there. It doesn't say specifically that it's from you. Did you draft this?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Item 1, and this matter was raised during your direct examination, about timing, timing of negotiations. And under item 1 you say: "Hadzic was probably right when he said that negotiations between the Croatian government and his regime had to start with confidence-building measures. He mentioned as such a cease-fire and first arrangements for practical co-operation." Now, do you remember that it was your view in June 1993 that, indeed, there was a need for confidence-building arrangements?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, all Serbs would tell us all the time that they had absolutely no confidence in the Croats. And, second, as long as there was a possibility of fighting, you could not easily consider any practical co-operation. So we had this three-tier approach. First, the cease-fire. Then an agreement on practical measures, such as opening electricity lines, pipelines, and roads. And then, third, a political solution. This was tried for years. It failed in the end and later we tried an overall approach, doing all three together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D98. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 01797, please; Prosecution tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is from Vollebaek and Ahrens, Zagreb, to Stoltenberg/Owen, Geneva. 23rd September 1993. Subject: Meetings with Mr. Hadzic and Mr. Jarcevic in Erdut and Foreign Minister Jovanovic in Belgrade, 23 September 1993. Did you draft this; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Vollebaek was very active on this Erdut 1 thing, so it could have been him. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Indeed, in paragraph 1 it does say: "Today I travelled together with Ambassador Ahrens to Erdut," so it seems that it was -- am I right --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Vollebaek, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why is Foreign Minister Jovanovic involved and what is he foreign minister of?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is foreign minister of that third Yugoslavia which had been set up in the spring of 1992 between Serbia and Montenegro. And since this was a very dangerous situation Tudjman wanted a solemn opening of his pontoon bridge, whereas the Serbs had let it be known that this was in the range of their artillery. This could have led to very severe consequences. And since we knew that, to put it mildly, that Belgrade had a certain influence on Knin, we talked to the Yugoslav foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And I'll read this paragraph in its entirety so that we have the full context, which is important: "Mr. Hadzic said that he fully accepted the idea and would be happy to participate since it was clear that the alternative was war. In fact, he pressed for an early start to the process because he feared further Croatian attacks in the near future." Let me stop there. Was there an attack that had occurred shortly before the 23rd of September, 1993, by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall when the Medak pocket attack was. That was under the point of view of human rights violations, war crimes, the worst of all. But it must have been somewhere in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say it was "worst of all," why do you say it was worst of all?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were killings of civilians and deliberate violations of human rights, not just by accidental fire or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you saying that the forces that engaged in that attack did that deliberately?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looked so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it your understanding they were under orders from someone to engage in those acts?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so because Tudjman understood that this would harm the position of his country. But there was, of course, an overall policy of not encouraging the Serbs to remain in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "On the question of return of displaced people, Ahrens mentioned that while in New York, the principle had been agreed that all displaced people should return, including Serbs to Croatian-held territory. Paspalj had said that no Serbs would want to go back. Hadzic said that the principle was correct, but then went on to say quite strongly that Serbs and Croats could never live together again. It might be possible for Croats to return to Krajina, but it was inconceivable for Serbs to want to return to Croatia." Now, is what Mr. Hadzic saying here about "never live together again," is that in reference to a desire that the RSK, or whatever Serb-held territories there might be, should not be reintegrated into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, that was actually one of the principles of the nationalist wing of Serbian politics, which, at that time, was the vast majority. And I remember that I went to Belgrade immediately after the Operation Storm, which was in August 1995, and I talked to Serbian refugees, a large number of Serbian refugees on Serbian soil, I was in Obrenovac, and asked them whether they were prepared to return to Croatia. And they said, We will never return if our areas are under Croatian government because the Croatians are a genocidal nation. This was the overall feeling but, of course, also the product of a constant propaganda. They had no other means of information, source of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So Mr. Hadzic is accurately describing the feelings of those Serbs who had been forced out or who had left those areas --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he is describing. He is actually stating that policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, what it says here is that: "It might be possible for Croats to return to Krajina, but it was inconceivable for Serbs to want to return to Croatia." So isn't he -- isn't the distinction that he is drawing here, that Croats can come back to Serbia or to the RSK, whereas it was inconceivable that Serbs would want to go back to areas under Croatian control?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, first of all, there was an obligation under the Vance Plan that the Croatian refugees could return into the RSK areas and that was not fulfilled at all. And when I took this up with Serb interlocutors, I was always told that this was too dangerous for the RSK because the Croats would send soldiers in disguise. The second point is that even in Croatia, no one was prepared to return to the RSK under the government it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And because there are, is it not true, a large number of people of Serbian ethnicity who have themselves been displaced from parts of Croatia who, frankly, are hostile toward non-Serbs and in particular Croats?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, quite a bit happened in the area of Zadar and also Pakrac, whereas there were other islands of Serb settlements, which I mentioned yesterday, where the Serbs still would live, but they complained to me that cars with loudspeakers would drive through their villages at night and threatening them. That was this Gorski Kotar area. So it was not pleasant to be a Serb in Tudjman's Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And those people regrettably, as a result of those experiences, would not want to return to Croatia ; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Because the number of refugees was much higher after Operation Storm. We are talking in dimensions of 200.000. And, actually, the Serb side had prepared the evacuation of the population in case of a Croatian attack. You can find this in the report by Mr. Mazowiecki, the former Polish prime minister who was in charge of a human rights commission by the UN, that looked into the situation in Yugoslavia. And he said that some people after Operation Flash which -- where the Croats took Sector West, had actually been forced to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My question, and I guess it wasn't clear, was whether those Serb -- people of Serb ethnicity who had suffered from the intimidation that you described earlier, those people would not be willing to return to Croat-held territories in 1992 and 1993, after they had left.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So, in that sense, Mr. Hadzic's description is correct.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. But I think it's not a description because I think he was also convinced that Serbs and Croats could not live together. And that is something I simply do not buy. I remember in Osijek and in Vukovar, particularly in Vukovar, we had almost half/half Croats and Serbs. The number of marriages between Croats and Serbs corresponded almost exactly to the statistics when you understand that nationality doesn't play a role. I talked to statisticians about this. It was quite interesting. And actually I witnessed marriages breaking up over the war, between Serbs and Croats. I have been told about this. I have not witnessed it myself in the form of the real break. So this -- this was what I called earlier in the day ethnic madness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 7733, starting at line 20 -- line 1: "Did Mr. Hadzic ever express the view to you that whatever the territory was, Serbian and Croatian people simply could not live together?" Your answer: "I cannot recall that Mr. Hadzic said that to me. Others did?"

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So it's not correct that Mr. Hadzic -- that you recalled that Mr. Hadzic told you that Serbs and Croats couldn't live together?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't say that. I say that I believe that was also his conviction because everyone, even the bishops surrounding the patriarch in Belgrade, said such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, over the course of your meetings, and you've testified to this with Mr. Hadzic -- well, first of all, let me ask you: How many times did you meet with him privately?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never met privately in the form that we arranged a meeting one on one. But in the framework of such meetings, I very often took the opportunity of talking one on one to the interlocutors, and I did so particularly often with Mr. Hadzic because we had developed a certain working relationship which made discussions fruitful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your observation that he was candid with you -- excuse me. Your observation was that he was candid with you on those occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some occasions, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday at page 7722 that you found it "remarkable that he did not object to me being German" in respect of your responsibilities as a mediator?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether "remarkable" is the right term but at least he did not do it. The Serbs, after a while, felt that I was not a Serb hater or something like that. I mean, I had very close relationships in Belgrade and I also used to go to the writers' club in Belgrade which was the centre of national Serbs. I would meet writers there. I knew Dobrica Cosic who became the president of the third Yugoslavia. I knew everyone. I also talked, of course, to Karadzic and Hadzic -- Mladic and Koljevic and whom have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in the course of either your private discussions with him at any time or otherwise, did Mr. Hadzic ever tell you that non-Serbs should be segregated from Serbs within the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not say that. I mean, it was quite clear that we were against ethnic cleansing, and when I raised questions of human rights, he would normally agree to the standards which they have in their laws and their constitution. But it was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he ever express to you the view that non-Serbs should be harassed?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he ever suggest to you that the non-Serbs should be forced out of the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it happened. While he was president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one more line of questioning, but I would prefer to start it after the break, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course. Your Excellency, this is the second break. As always, 30 minutes, which means we come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, while that's taking place, I can take care of the first three pages of 65 ter 1681, which have now been uploaded as 1D00732.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Excellency, you testified yesterday in relation to the Norway negotiations that you believe that Mr. Hadzic leaked the existence of those negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was said at the conference and that was the common conviction. I think there's a factual basis to it, but I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say you don't know which, what do you not know?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly which media he informed at what point in time. And what he told them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is the basis of your information about the leak solely the information that was provided by Mr. Sarinic during the closing session?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think Vollebaek, who was very much in charge there in Norway, also checked it but I cannot say that for sure. I even had the feeling that the Serb side did not contest this, that they agreed that Mr. Hadzic had gone public. But, as I said, I say with much reserve. This is 20 years ago and I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was there an ongoing issue in the negotiations that the Croats would send the lowest possible representative of government whereas the Serb side would frequently be represented by the president himself?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this was, of course, one of the points that constantly played a role. We mentioned yesterday that in Borovo Selo the main issue was how Mr. Hadzic was to sign. The international community did not recognise that Mr. Hadzic was the president of an existing state because the state was not recognised. And Mr. Sarinic was a quite high-ranking Croatian official, I think one who was quite well placed to deal with it and we appreciated him to some others who were not always as professional in negotiations. It is correct that if you take Mr. Hadzic's position as president, then Sarinic was not up to him, but Tudjman would never have sat opposite Mr. Hadzic. Then you wouldn't have any talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall what Mr. Sarinic's position was?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was some sort of advisor to the -- to the president, something like head of the presidential administration. I can't tell you exactly but it was a position of power. He had more power than a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can go please to P2889; Prosecution tab 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is the document you looked at, Your Excellency, in relation to this meeting during your direct testimony. If we turn the page to item 4, Sarinic says if he had been correctly informed, the head of the Serb delegation was giving a television interview, so he had put that above the Plenary Session.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's the second-last sentence.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of number 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, is that the leak?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think there was a second step. There was first the leak and then later the interview. If I recall well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is what you recall that, first, Hadzic makes some kind of -- gives some kind of a leak and then he goes off and gives a television interview somewhere, about the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be that the leak had been rather earlier. Maybe one day earlier. And then these negotiations failed. And it had become public, and so it was only logical that Hadzic, as leader of the delegation, would give then an interview. There was no more secret. If this is so, I cannot exactly retell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As best you can recall or perhaps you can't at all recall but did this interview, supposed interview occur in Norway?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if I recall well, it was some sort of telephone conversation or something like that with a journalist who went public and certainly with a Serbian media, not with the Norwegian media.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Sarinic's allegation is that Mr. Hadzic is giving a television interview.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the second -- the second point. Because Sarinic bitterly complained about Mr. Hadzic not being present at the last Plenary Session of the negotiating group and I think he said at this press conference connection with this absence of Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday he might have gone shopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's just stick with what's written here and the allegation.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is the allegation, then, that Mr. Hadzic is giving a television interview to Serb media in Norway?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understand this passage. Vollebaek is still alive. He will be able to say it more exactly. I think I should not go beyond this because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, given Mr. Hadzic's position that we've seen in some of the previous documents and the allegations that had arisen in his regard, how do you think it would have played amongst a domestic audience if it turned out -- or, for that matter, amongst RSK Assembly members if it turned out that Goran Hadzic was engaged in direct face-to-face meetings with the Croats secretly? Would that be to his benefit?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would assume that the Serb leadership, particularly including Belgrade, were aware of this meeting even when it was secret, and it was always popular to say that a meeting with the Croats had failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was it popular to say that one was engaging in secret meetings with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one would try one's best and, I mean, Mile Novakovic was there. There were quite a few people there so it was not just Mr. Hadzic alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that answers the question but let me put it differently. How would this play amongst Assembly members in the RSK who surely would not have all been informed about secret negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hard-liners would certainly not be too pleased. On the other hand, the aims of the Serbs in these talks was, number one, what they said, peace. It is definitely peaceful relations on the border as they see it. And, number two, facilitating certain activities and economic measures that would greatly help the population. And, number three, insisting on the RSK never joining Croatia. These were the three points which, if put properly, would convince the audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The hard-liners, of course, would have no interest in putting things properly, would they?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which things? These three points?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The beneficial aspects of engaging in such negotiations.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. There might have been a certain - how shall I say? - fatigue of tension and of insecurity which might have convinced a number of Serbs that it might be about to time to come to terms with the Croats, in particular, as they had been made believe that there is a possibility of having a -- an agreed future outside of Croatia. That's what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Anything in re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador Ahrens. Just a few questions to follow up on some of those put to you by my learned friend, Mr. Gosnell. At the beginning of the cross-examination, you were asked a series of questions referring to various national movements of self-determination. Slovenia, Slovakia and some other countries were referred to. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know or could you give us an indication what percentage of Slovenia was constituted by Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact percentage but it is very high, around 90 or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yeah. Any idea the percentage of Slovaks in what became Slovakia when that country split?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I think it was also quite high. And they were not so much mixed with Czechs as with Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you have a general idea of the percentage of Serbs who were living in Croatia during these times?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 11.5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, again, you've already given some numbers about the various percentages in the Sector East.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In particular, Vukovar had 37 per cent Serbs and 44 per cent Croats and that was the highest percentage in Sector East of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So when talking about national movements of self-determination, is there any distinction to be made between those that occurred in places like Slovenia versus Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, definitely so when it comes to Croatia, the Sector East was -- had no Serb majority whatsoever. And that is why, for example, the Z-4 plan which provided for autonomy for the Krajina did not provide such an autonomy for Sector East, just a few points, but not this very wide-reaching autonomy provided for Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you agreed with the proposal put to you by Mr. Gosnell that crimes need not be committed as part of a national movement for self-determination. I wonder if you have a view as to the likelihood of crimes occurring when such a national movement is being undertaken by a group that's in a significant minority in that country.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it's difficult to answer that question. But it's quite clear that there's no legitimacy to such a movement when they are only a minority. And if they want to impose their will on the majority, the motive to use unacceptable means are, of course, stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we have, please, what's now been marked, I believe, as Defence Exhibit 1D713. This was the 8th of November, 1991 letter from Rome, or from the conference in Rome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ambassador Ahrens, you were asked to comment on this document during your cross-examination, and I just would briefly take you back to it at page 3, in paragraph 25. And if -- thank you. And again, focussing on the fifth paragraph that we see here, which I believe is the one that counsel referred you to already: "... prospect of recognition of the independence of those republics wishing it can be only be envisaged in the framework of an overall settlement and includes adequate guarantees for the protection of human rights, rights of national or ethnic groups. They urge parties concerned to prepare forthwith legal provisions to that [sic] end." Now the question here, Ambassador, is yesterday on your direct, we looked at the constitutional law on minorities for Croatia. Is that something that was envisaged here in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly one of the backgrounds and that is also one of the reasons why we were so active with this constitutional law, although the Krajina Serbs were not prepared to consider such a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And now this is the 8th of November, 1991. But in your cross-examination, you mentioned the impact of Vukovar, and the question there would be, if you could elaborate on that. The fall of Vukovar and the events surrounding it, did that have an impact on the prospects that any sort of overall settlement might still encompass a Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, these semantic exercise about a Yugoslavia were, rather, not very fruitful because a Yugoslavia that would have been a confederation was not acceptable to the Serbs. So the problems in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina would have arisen even if Tudjman's Croatia and Izetbegovic's Bosnia had joined a confederation. The Serbs wanted a federation. And Milosevic's policy before the fighting was in the direction of a centralisation of the country and not a confederalisation of the country so that -- that -- this is a little bit a remainder of the general feeling of regret that Yugoslavia fell apart. I said before no one wanted that, but it was not to be prevented in any way anymore at this time. And Vukovar really put the seal under this because Vukovar became very prominent in the media, in Western media, and this then became, of course, also an important argument for politicians who wanted to be popular in their own countries. But it is correct that Lord Carrington was against recognition to the end and he later said that recognition had ruined his conference, but this I don't know in how far because what we needed were Serb concessions and not Croat concessions. And I have seen that particularly in the Bosnian context, that pressure was also put on the weaker part because they had to make concessions and not on the stronger parts, so that Milosevic got away with a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just to round this out, because we're talking about the events surrounding Vukovar in November of 1991, there have been references today to Slovenia. And just so it's in the record, the Chamber recalls, were you aware of events that occurred in Slovenia involving the JNA and then the status of Slovenia in respect of a unified Yugoslavia as of this time, November 1991?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, Slovenia had been a theatre of fighting in end of June until the 3rd of July, I think. By mid-July, there was the so-called Brioni agreement by which Slovenia and Croatia postponed their independence by three months. It was an agreement with the EC. And the mandate of the ECMM originally was to observe whether independence had really been postponed. So I remember the rather senseless activity of going to the border posts of Yugoslavia with Hungary and Italy and Austria to see whether there was still the Yugoslav flag with the red star in the middle or not. If it was not there, then that was a breach of Brioni. In the meantime, when we were in our ridiculous white dresses in Zagreb, people in the street would attack us and say, You go to these -- these border posts and have your coffee there while our people are dying in the conflict zones --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So just to get in the record the year, you mention the 3rd of July. Would that be 1991?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So as of that time - I don't know how to characterise it - in a sort of de facto way, anyway, Slovenia is already out?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, on the 3rd of July, I think the fighting stopped. By mid-July was the Brian agreement and postponement of independence by three months. Three months later, both Tudjman and Kucan proclaimed independence anew. And sometime, I don't know the exact date, the -- Belgrade decided to withdraw the JNA from Slovenia --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and this was then carried out but they remained in Croatia where we then had the siege of the JNA barracks by Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well. Now coming back to November 1991, the date of this document. At that time, again, the reference to an overall settlement, by that point in time what were the prospects that an overall settlement was going to involve a change of borders so that all Serbs could live in one country?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Because the treaty provisions for the convention did not provide for this and it was in the international community a really -- really a non-subject because at the same time the Soviet Union broke apart and it was the Russians who insisted very much on borders to be preserved. And I remember that my good friend Leonid Kerestedzhiyants, who used to be the Russian ambassador in Zagreb, during those years after Russian recognition was not welcome in Knin because they considered him anti-RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, today in your evidence - I'm looking at page 16 of today's transcript, roughly around line 14 - you were looking at the Vance Plan. And the language about special arrangements in these areas would of an interim nature and would not prejudge the outcome of political negotiations for a comprehensive settlement of the Yugoslav crisis. And then you were being asked whether this implied or could be understood as some possibility of a -- of a final status. Your answer was that the lines - this is the PAs - were meant to define the responsibilities of the conference -- sorry, not the PAs. But define the responsibilities of the conference on one side, which was still Carrington conference, and UNPROFOR to be deployed. So that they could -- sorry, so they should create the conditions under which the conference would then negotiate the final settlement. And you -- that's your reference there that I'm interested in is the statement that UNPROFOR, the indication UNPROFOR was to create the conditions under which final settlement could be achieved. The question, Ambassador, is: What was the likelihood that -- well, was UNPROFOR ever able to create those conditions that were envisioned, particularly in respect of demobilisation?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the picture which we have very often when they would send troops abroad. A certain number of troops is requested and much less are being sent and then this cannot be done. In Lord Owen's book you'll find this for Srebrenica, where they made this mistake in a very tragic -- with tragic consequences. And this was at least the idea, and Vance and then -- his -- Ambassador Okun and the -- the -- the UN administration felt that this could be brought about. The conference on Yugoslavia, the EC conference, there was definitely a wish by the Dutch, by -- by Foreign Minister van den Broek to come to a final solution before the end of 1991. They wanted to do this before Christmas. And in one of the press conferences and declarations, somewhere in November it was even said that if there was no final solution until that time recognition would be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. On page 20 of today's transcript, you were being asked about specifically do you have any knowledge or understanding about the relative authority of Mr. Hadzic versus the JNA commanders who were present in the territory. And you said that you did not have such knowledge or understanding. You did talk, however, about having met Mr. Hadzic in Borovo Selo in September of 1991. If I recall correctly, your evidence was that there was officer of the JNA who was also present?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, this officer had come together with us to Borovo Selo across the Danube. This is not something which I had recalled but I think I have seen it in one of the -- the -- the films which was shown to me. Then he would have come together with us from Belgrade or have been on the other side of the Danube in Serbia. But this military officer is seen greeting in that film with Mr. Hadzic and then he sat in in our negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And did he play any other role or -- I guess, the ultimate question: Who signed? Did he sign or did Mr. Hadzic sign --

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think he didn't say a word, or very little. He just sat there. And what we needed was Mr. Hadzic's signature. Not the signature of that general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have P2889.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ambassador, we just looked at this a few minutes ago with my learned friend. This relates to the Norway negotiations in November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could move to paragraph 4 and 5 on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were just asked some questions about the -- the suggestions or the indication that there had been a leak and a breach of the security. If we could focus on paragraph 5, here it's recorded a person named Rakic is speaking on behalf of the Serb delegation.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a military from the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He indicated that he believed it was -- well, that the president of the RSK not being present was -- was -- he was justifiably not present because there had been apparently some confusion about the time. And then also the point that's already been alluded to about the president was not sitting opposite his equal in rank. Now, this was the third and final day of negotiations. Had Mr. Hadzic been present on the previous days?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And would -- do you know if the rest of his delegation was informed of the time that the Plenary was to take place here on the last day?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how the Serb delegation was informed at that time. But when the Serbs said that their president was not sitting opposite his equal in rank, then the intention was always to bust the negotiations because it was 100 per cent sure that the Croats would not send their president to sit with the Serbs from Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That may have answered my next and my last question, which, having engaged in so many negotiations with so many leaders, what would have been the impact of the head of the delegation not even appearing on the final day's Plenary?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it was, I think, just a protocolarian impact and not a political impact because at that time, the negotiations had already come to an unsuccessful end. There's, of course, one point. This was the last months of Hadzic's presidency and I don't know in how far he was already aware of the fact that he would be replaced by the, as I see it, more radical Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very -- two, three months thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just have two questions on redirect arising out of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you were just asked about the person, the JNA officer who accompanied you to Borovo Selo on the 6th of September. And you said that: He would have coming to -- with us from Belgrade or have been on the other side of the Danube in Serbia. Is my understanding correct that he was escorting you either from Belgrade or from Serbia to Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. And I must say this was not my recollection. I have seen this here on one of these films that he shook hands with Mr. Hadzic coming from somewhere. I don't even know for sure whether he came with us across the Danube or from somewhere else. But at least he had not been stationed where we had these talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you had no indication that he was the JNA commander in the area, did you?

utterances.speaker: GEERT AHRENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met the JNA commander in the area. That was the Osijek one. I don't think whether that was the same area, but maybe that was the event of the 5th of October, the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your Excellency, this is the end of your testimony. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. I'm -- I must say that, and I'm speaking for myself because I didn't confer with my colleagues, that your testimony was very helpful in -- as I understood it. So thank you very much. You're now released as a witness. We wish you a safe journey home. The court usher will escort you out of the court. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. If you allow me one procedural point. I see this protocol here, this running protocol on the screen, and in two instances I think the Defence and you yourself have told me that there was an obvious error. There may be more such errors so I cannot authorise this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You are -- one, you are not authorising it, Ambassador. And two, this -- this draft transcript is reviewed by persons behind --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I was -- thought so. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- so it will improve. By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me for the remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, is -- would it be useful to have the next witness, if is he -- he or she is -- is it a he or a she?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's a he.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's a he.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He arrived last night after an overnight trip, Mr. President, and with the Court's permission, we would prefer to start tomorrow. He is a relatively short witness, under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No problem by that. So then the court is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
